newsitem.title: USA: Wheat prices fall sharply, coffee rises.
newsitem.headline: Wheat prices fall sharply, coffee rises.

text.p: Wheat prices fell sharply on Monday after rains fell in parched areas of the European wheat belt, easing worries about the threat of drought.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat for May delivery closed 11-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $4.12. At the Kansas City Board of Trade, hard red winter wheat for May delivery ended down a sharp 21 cents at $4.49 a bushel.
"Weekend rains in Europe were a little better than we thought they were going to be," said Dale Gustafson, a Smith Barney grain analyst.
Rain fell over the weekend in western Europe and in France, with agronomists there saying the moisture would boost crop prospects. More rains were forecast for this week.

Crop prospects also improved in the United States, with drier weather in the spring wheat growing region of Minnesota and the Dakotas improving planting conditions. The hard red winter wheat belt from Texas to Kansas, which was hit by a damaging freeze two weeks ago, also saw good weekend weather.
Corn prices fell back as cool, clear weather in the Midwest allowed rapid planting progress. Corn for May delivery closed 3-3/4 cents a bushel lower at $2.90-3/4.
The Agriculture Department said after the market closed that 18 percent of corn acreage had been planted as of Sunday compared to 15 percent on average for the last five years.

Selling pressure in corn also was tied to a weekly report by the Agriculture Department showing 30.3 million bushels were inspected for export shipments last week, on the low end of trade expectations for 29 to 35 million bushels.

Strong exports of soybeans, on the other hand, supported prices. Soybeans for May delivery ended 1/2 cent a bushel higher at $8.68-1/4 after news that 18.9 million bushels of soybeans were inspected for export, twice the prior week's level.

"We're still not seeing signs of rationing in the crush number or the export pace," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities, referring to the weekly demand from processors who crush soybeans into meal and oils.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee futures ended mostly higher with traders remaining nervous about tight stocks at roasters and supplies later this year.
Coffee for May delivery closed up 3.90 cents a pound at 220.25 cents.
A steady decline of U.S. warehouse stocks of certified for delivery against futures from more than 83,000 bags three weeks ago has helped fuel supply jitters.
On Friday the exchange reported that certified coffee stocks fell another 1,747 bags to 48,603 bags as of April 24.
Each bag contains 132 pounds of coffee.
"The likelihood is that there is going to be some squeeze between now and mid-May," said Refco analyst Ann Prendergast.
"I expect there will be extreme volatility and rising prices from delivery fears," she added.

A forecaster at Brazil's National Institute of Meteorology also said on Monday that the country's winter should not be as cold as last year's. But he would not rule out frosts hitting coffee, with the greatest risk from late June through July.
"This should not be a harsh winter this year, temperatures should be more or less normal, but there is still the risk of frosts in the coffee areas," said forecaster Francisco Assis.
Brazil is the world's top coffee grower and exporter.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices edged lower in quiet trade as the market awaited fresh news.
Crude oil for June delivery closed 8 cents a barrel lower at $19.91 and unleaded gaasoline for May delivery closed down 0.16 cent a gallon at 62.34 cents.

Political violence in Nigeria's Warri oil-producing region, which forced producer Royal Dutch/Shell Group last week to delay several April and May shipments, has kept a floor under prices. But the disruption has not been enough to lift an oversupplied market, traders said.

"We're stuck in a range -- sellers are cautious because of of the Shell Nigeria situation but buyers are wary with (technical) resistance nearby," said Thomas Blakeslee, an oil trader at Cargill Investor Services in New York.
Crude oil, after slumping 30 percent in the first quarter, has traded between roughly $19 and $20.50 over the past month.
May heating oil closed up 0.63 cent a gallon at 56.53 cents in technical trade ahead of Wedesday's contract expiration. All other heating oil contracts closed lower.
